name: Sulaymaniyah Tablet V: a new manuscript of Tablet V of the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh (Sulaymaniyah Museum, T.1447)
date: Acquired late 2011 by the Sulaymaniyah Museum (Slemani, Kurdistan Region of Iraq); published June 2014 in the Journal of Cuneiform Studies 66 [uncertain: volume and page range, commonly cited as JCS 66 (2014), pp. 69-90]; wide press coverage in September-October 2015 (Live Science, Smithsonian, Biblical Archaeology Society, Ancient History Encyclopedia). Tablet itself dated on script to the Neo-Babylonian period (626-539 BCE), probably not later than the 6th century BCE
creator: Farouk N. H. Al-Rawi (identified the tablet and advised the purchase) and Andrew R. George (SOAS, University of London), co-authors of 'Back to the Cedar Forest: The Beginning and End of Tablet V of the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgameš'. Institution: Sulaymaniyah Museum, director Hashim Hama Abdullah; visit supported by Hero Talabani. Photographs widely circulated by Osama S. M. Amin
form: Physical clay tablet in cuneiform, about 11 x 9.5 x 3 cm, made from three fragments already joined when acquired; preserves the beginning and end of Tablet V. Published as a scholarly article with hand-copy, transliteration, translation and commentary
effect_on_arc: Changes the Cedar Forest episode from a monster-slaying into something closer to a crime. The forest is no longer a silent wilderness: it is a dense, fragrant jungle full of birds, cicadas and screaming monkeys, a noise George called a 'symphony (or cacophony)'. Humbaba stops reading as a barbarian ogre and starts reading as a foreign ruler whose court is entertained by this music, 'in the manner of Babylonian kings'. The tablet also strengthens the reading that Enkidu and Humbaba knew each other before [uncertain: how much the new lines add to what Tablet V already implied], which makes the killing a betrayal. At the end of the tablet Enkidu voices guilt: 'we have reduced the forest [to] a wasteland', and he dreads Enlil asking what wrath drove them to trample it. That prepares the ground for the gods' verdict and Enkidu's death in Tablet VII, so the heroes' triumph now carries a clear moral and ecological cost
critical_response: Treated by Assyriologists as a solid, significant addition to the Standard Babylonian text, fixing the opening and close of Tablet V and adding about twenty lines. George's own framing (Cedar Forest as 'a dense jungle inhabited by exotic and noisy fauna'; Humbaba as a cultured ruler) was taken up widely by the popular press in 2015 (Live Science, Smithsonian 'Smart News', Biblical Archaeology Society, Ancient History Encyclopedia/World History Encyclopedia) as proof that the epic still has 'new' material. Later translators and retellers cite the tablet as a source of fresh Cedar Forest material [uncertain: which specific translations incorporate it]
controversies: Provenance: the museum bought the tablet from a known antiquities smuggler, one of a batch of 80-90 objects, for about $800. The museum defended its policy of paying smugglers to keep objects in Iraq rather than letting them leave the country, but critics of such purchases argue they reward looting. Findspot is unknown [uncertain: speculation about a southern Iraqi site, possibly Babylon or Borsippa, is unverified]. Dating: the museum label called it Old Babylonian (2003-1595 BCE) while George dated the script to the Neo-Babylonian period; press reports repeated both dates
regional_reception: The object stays in Iraq, held by the Sulaymaniyah Museum in the Kurdistan Region, and Iraqi Kurdish officials presented the purchase as a rescue of Iraqi heritage. The discovery was reported in Arabic and Kurdish media [uncertain: extent of regional coverage]. A rare case of a major Gilgamesh find made and kept in the region rather than in a Western collection
method: Traditional cuneiform scholarship: Al-Rawi recognised the text among smuggled tablets; he and George read and collated the tablet in the museum over about five days, identified it as Tablet V of the Standard Babylonian epic by matching it against known manuscripts, and published a hand-copy, transliteration and translation. The three pieces were already physically joined
ai_pipeline_stage: None. Identification, reading and translation were entirely human
scale_metrics: One tablet, three joined fragments, about 11 x 9.5 x 3 cm; about 20 previously unknown lines added to Tablet V, plus better readings of lines already partly known; Neo-Babylonian manuscript (626-539 BCE); purchase price about $800, from a batch of 80-90 tablets
what_was_found: The beginning and end of Tablet V of the Standard Babylonian epic: Gilgamesh and Enkidu arrive at the Cedar Forest and see the cedars dripping aromatic sap and hear the din of birds, cicadas and monkeys; Humbaba's court music; and, after the killing, Enkidu's lament over the ruined forest and his fear of Enlil's anger. Sits between the journey (Tablet IV) and the heroes' return to Uruk and Ishtar's proposal (Tablet VI)
provenance_and_ethics: Almost certainly looted, sold by a smuggler; findspot unknown. Held legitimately by the Sulaymaniyah Museum (T.1447), which bought it under a policy of intercepting antiquities before they leave Iraq. Photographs are public (Osama S. M. Amin, World History Encyclopedia); the scholarly edition is in the Journal of Cuneiform Studies. No repatriation needed since it never left Iraq, which contrasts with the Gilgamesh Dream Tablet returned from the US in 2021
ai_craft_tension: No machine touched this find. A scholar had to recognise a Gilgamesh passage among dozens of smuggled tablets, and another had to read a damaged Neo-Babylonian script and see what the new lines did to the story. The telling part is interpretive: noticing that monkeys and cicadas turn Humbaba into a king with a court orchestra, and that Enkidu's 'wasteland' line gives the killing a moral cost. Today's fragment-matching tools (such as the Fragmentarium) could plausibly have flagged the text as Tablet V faster [uncertain: counterfactual], but deciding what it means for Humbaba and Enkidu remains a reader's job. It is a useful baseline case: the pre-AI way of recovering Gilgamesh, still producing major results in the 2010s
essay_hooks: An $800 purchase from a smuggler added about twenty lines to the world's oldest epic (World History Encyclopedia). Monkeys in the Cedar Forest: George called the forest 'a dense jungle inhabited by exotic and noisy fauna' and its sound 'a symphony (or cacophony)' (Biblical Archaeology Society). Humbaba recast from ogre to 'a foreign ruler entertained with exotic music at court' (World History Encyclopedia). Enkidu's guilt: 'we have reduced the forest [to] a wasteland' (Biblical Archaeology Society). Contrast: a 2,500-year-old ecological lament, found with no machine help, set against AI-assisted recoveries of the 2020s
